questions.question_text:
Explain the difference between a process and a thread.

(0) Define a process and a thread, and state their basic relationship.
(a) What resources does a process own that threads of the same process typically share?
(b) What does each thread have of its own?
(c) Give one advantage of using multiple threads inside one process instead of multiple processes.
(d) Give one disadvantage or risk of multithreading compared with separate processes.
questions.reference_answer:
A process is an independent program instance; threads are concurrent execution units within a process.
(a) Threads in the same process typically share the process address space: code, data/heap, and open OS resources such as file descriptors (and often the same PID-level resources).
(b) Each thread has its own stack, register context / program counter, and thread-local scheduling state (thread ID).
(c) Advantage: cheaper context switch / shared memory communication is easy — creating threads and sharing data is lighter than creating processes and using IPC.
(d) Disadvantage: one buggy thread can corrupt shared memory and crash the whole process; also needs synchronization (races). Separate processes give stronger isolation.
questions.rubric:
Total 5 marks (1 mark each):
1) Core distinction: a process is an independent running program/program instance with its own resource boundary; a thread is an execution unit within a process. Award 0.5 if only one side is defined or the relationship is merely implied.
2) Shared by threads of one process: address space / code+data/heap / open files (any clear statement of shared memory space).
3) Per-thread private: stack and/or registers/PC/thread context.
4) Advantage: lighter weight, faster create/switch, easy shared-memory communication (any one clear advantage).
5) Disadvantage: weaker isolation / shared-memory bugs / need locks; process isolation is safer (any one clear risk).
Partial credit (0.5) if partially correct.
Award 0 if absent, confuses process with CPU core only, or contradictory.

student_answers.answer_text:
(a) Threads of the same process share the process address space — code, heap/data, and usually open file descriptors.
(b) Each thread keeps its own stack, registers, and program counter (its own execution context).
(c) Multithreading is lighter: creating a thread and sharing data in memory is cheaper than multiple processes plus IPC.
(d) Risk: a bad thread can overwrite shared memory and crash the whole process; you also need locks to avoid races. Separate processes isolate faults better.

Process owns the address space that sibling threads share (code + data).
Each thread has a private stack and register set.
Advantage of threads: faster context switch and easy shared-memory cooperation.
Disadvantage: no strong isolation — one thread fault can take down all threads in the process; synchronization required.
